newsitem.title: CHINA: China seen unlikely to cut interest rates soon.
newsitem.headline: China seen unlikely to cut interest rates soon.

text.p: China's financial tsars have shelved a plan to pull interest rates down another notch early this year due to fears that surging fixed asset investment, will get out of hand, bankers and traders said on Wednesday.

Domestic financial markets reacted positively to signals from Beijing late last year that another interest rate cut was imminent. Those markets, however, are now digesting a new message that rates are likely to remain unchanged.
A Beijing-based banker said authorities feared an inflationary backlash from a resurgence in fixed asset investment in the second half of 1996 following two earlier interest rate cuts.
"There is the need to maintain austerity measures," the banker said. "Another bank interest rate cut is unlikely in the short term as a result."
The banker quoted official figures as showing that local governments around China had approved more than 1,000 fixed asset investment projects since July last year.

The expectations of a rate cut had been based largely on China's lower-than-expected retail price inflation of 6.1 percent year-on-year in 1996 against a year-on-year 14.8 percent in 1995, analysts said.
Bankers said the heaviest pressure for another cut has come from poorly-managed state-run enterprises, starved of cash due to tight credit policies in place since 1993.
But Beijing has made it clear that the two interest rate cuts are all the relief state firms can expect on the financial front for now, and they must work to improve their management, they said.

"We're still expecting a rate cut but not immediately," said an analyst with a foreign brokerage in Shanghai. "It may come late in the second quarter, but a lot depends on what happens with the state enterprises."
The analyst said the central bank's inclination was to leave interest rates alone longer, but the huge debt burden carried by the state enterprises was pressuring them to reconsider.
"I think a lot of the 1996 annual results of these companies are going to be ugly, largely because of the interest charges they are bearing. So maybe they say: 'time for another cut'," he said.
To help state enterprises deal with the problem, the central People's Bank of China is making changes to improve the flow of funds to them to offset the interest burden.

Last week, state banks were ordered to gradually pull out of the state debt secondary market to guide short-term bank money into the state firms instead of going into the stock markets, analysts said.
Beijing has also approved a doubling of the amount of corporate bonds and shares to be issued this year compared to last year to help more firms raise money, they added.
"As a key part of China's finance reforms, the central government seems determined to drive the state firms to rely more on the markets," said a second trader.
